topic: Classes, Objects, Members and Nested Classes
q: What is an object in C++?
opts: A data type of the class
More than one of the above
exp: A class is the plan; an object is one instance made from that plan. Like Python's Car(), C++ can create many separate Car objects. A method belongs to a class, but is not itself the object.
concept: Turn the blueprint metaphor into concrete declarations. Separate a class definition, an object, a pointer/reference, and a method call.

source.explanation:
) An instance of the class
Explanation: An object in C++ is a runtime entity that represents an instance of a class. It is created based on the
blueprint defined by the class and holds specific data and methods associated with that class. Objects allow the program
to interact with the class's attributes and functions. While the class defines the structure, the object is the tangible entity
that uses this structure.

q: Where is memory allocated for objects in C++?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the simplified exam model, live objects use working memory (RAM), not read-only ROM. Automatic objects and dynamically allocated objects have different storage durations. concept: Separate the object's lifetime from the lifetime of a pointer variable. This prevents many of the most serious mistakes in the assignments.

source.explanation:
) RAM
Explanation: Memory for objects in C++ is allocated in RAM. This memory allocation can happen on the stack or heap,
depending on how the object is created. Objects created using the new keyword are allocated on the heap, while local
objects are stored in the stack. RAM provides the working memory necessary for executing programs and storing
runtime data.

q:
What determines when a variable comes into existence
in memory?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The key selects D, but the wording confuses scope with lifetime. Scope tells where a name is visible; storage duration and initialization govern when its object exists. A data type determines representation, not by itself the moment of creation. Learn the distinction rather than treating all three as interchangeable.

source.explanation:

Explanation: The existence of a variable in memory depends on multiple factors:
• Data type: Determines the size and type of data the variable can store.
• Storage class: Specifies the variable's lifetime and visibility (e.g., auto, static, extern).
• Scope: Defines the region in the code where the variable is accessible.
Together, these factors govern the variable's lifecycle, allocation, and accessibility.

Calls made from main() are not inherently tied to virtual dispatch unless a polymorphic call is explicitly made.
Thus, both A and B are correct, making D the right answer.
